items.followUp: State one ecological role of a keystone predator in a marine ecosystem.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the population-control role of starfish.
rubric.description: Starfish control populations of organisms such as mussels.
rubric.how: Name a prey population and state that starfish control its numbers.

rubric.why: Award for linking this control to ecosystem health.
rubric.description: This helps maintain balance and biodiversity in the sea ecosystem.
rubric.how: State that regulating prey helps maintain ecosystem balance or biodiversity.

modelAnswer: Starfish prey on organisms such as mussels and help control their populations.
This prevents one species from dominating and helps maintain balance and biodiversity in the sea ecosystem.

items.followUp: How does mitosis help heal a wound?

rubric.why: Award for explaining what mitosis produces.
rubric.description: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells.
rubric.how: State that the new cells are identical to the original body cell.

rubric.why: Award for connecting mitosis to cell replacement in the body.
rubric.description: The new cells replace damaged or worn-out cells and repair tissues.
rubric.how: Explain that mitosis supplies cells for replacement or repair.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells genetically identical to the parent body cell.
These cells replace worn-out or damaged cells and help repair body tissues.

items.followUp: Explain how fertilisation restores the diploid chromosome number.

rubric.why: Award for explaining how the chromosome number is reduced before fertilisation.
rubric.description: Meiosis forms haploid gametes with half the chromosome number.
rubric.how: State that meiosis halves the chromosome number in gametes.

rubric.why: Award for explaining how the normal number is restored.
rubric.description: At fertilisation, two haploid gametes fuse and restore the diploid number.
rubric.how: State that fusion of the gametes restores the diploid chromosome number.

modelAnswer: Meiosis produces haploid gametes, each having half the chromosome number of the parent.
At fertilisation, two haploid gametes fuse and restore the diploid chromosome number in the offspring.

items.followUp: Describe what happens to the rate of photosynthesis as light intensity increases.

rubric.why: Award for stating the initial effect of increasing carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.description: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis, while carbon dioxide is limiting.
rubric.how: State that the rate rises as carbon dioxide concentration rises.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the levelling-off at high concentration.
rubric.description: The increase eventually levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.how: State that beyond a certain concentration the rate does not rise further.

modelAnswer: As carbon dioxide concentration increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases while carbon dioxide is a limiting factor.
At high concentrations, the rate levels off because another factor becomes limiting.

items.followUp: What happens to chlorophyll molecules when they absorb light in the light-dependent reactions?

rubric.why: Award for the light-absorbing role of photosystems.
rubric.description: Pigments in photosystems absorb light energy.
rubric.how: State that photosystem pigments capture light energy.

rubric.why: Award for explaining what the absorbed energy initiates.
rubric.description: The energy excites electrons and initiates the light-dependent reactions.
rubric.how: Link absorbed light energy to electron excitation or the light reactions.

modelAnswer: Photosystems contain pigment molecules that absorb light energy.
This energy excites electrons in the reaction centre and starts the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

items.followUp: Give one example each of an intracellular enzyme and an extracellular enzyme.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing enzymes that act outside cells.
rubric.description: Extracellular enzymes are released from cells and act outside them.
rubric.how: State that these enzymes are secreted and act outside the cell.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing enzymes that act within cells.
rubric.description: Intracellular enzymes act inside the cells in which they are made.
rubric.how: State that these enzymes function within the cell.

modelAnswer: Extracellular enzymes are secreted by cells and act outside the cells, for example digestive enzymes in the gut.
Intracellular enzymes act inside the cells in which they are produced.

items.followUp: What happens to an enzyme's activity when it is heated above its optimum temperature?

rubric.why: Award for identifying the structural effect of high temperature.
rubric.description: High temperature denatures the enzyme and changes the shape of its active site.
rubric.how: State that the enzyme or its active site changes shape due to denaturation.

rubric.why: Award for stating the effect on enzyme function.
rubric.description: The substrate no longer fits properly, so enzyme activity decreases or stops.
rubric.how: State that the reaction slows down or stops.

modelAnswer: Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme becomes denatured and its active site changes shape.
The substrate no longer fits the active site, so enzyme activity decreases or stops.

items.followUp: Define chyme and state where it is formed.

rubric.why: Award for the definition of bolus.
rubric.description: A bolus is chewed food mixed with saliva in the mouth.
rubric.how: Describe bolus as chewed food mixed with saliva.

rubric.why: Award for the definition of chyme.
rubric.description: Chyme is the semi-liquid mixture of partially digested food and gastric juice formed in the stomach.
rubric.how: Describe chyme as food mixed with gastric juice in the stomach.

modelAnswer: A bolus is chewed food mixed with saliva in the mouth before swallowing.
Chyme is the semi-liquid mixture of partially digested food and gastric juice formed in the stomach.
